Your goal in schmups is not to just beat them.

The whole genre comes from the Arcades, and that is how most Acrade games worked back then. You're supposed to be able to beat them in one sitting, but they're so hard it's damn near impossible so you have to put in a lot of quarters. It's useful because A:They were mostly highscore based, so meant to be replayed, B: It was probably hard to make long games back then, and C: this means one machine could only be used for like an hour max. And even if highscore wasn't that important, it was still often there and thus designed similarly.

In Shmups, at first it's all about learning to beat the game at all. Stage 2 is to beat it with little credits as possible. In 3 you try to do that for higher difficulties if they exist. The last stage is going for score, in which you not only try to beat it without dying, but also get the highest score you can. These games are meant to have tons of replayed playthroughs to perfect scores, so if they'd be really long, you'd get bored retrying. Each run is a new attempt at getting better at the game. Sometimes these scoring systems get extremely complex, despite the simplistic gameplay.

Note: I'm just speculating. I'm not entirely sure if I'm correct, as I've only casually played these games, but otherwise you could try asking fanatics over at http://shmups.system11.org/.

(Btw, I find it funny the other posts seem to think you're talking about FPS, haha)

shmups are usually pretty intense and unforgiving, it would be pretty stressful if they went on too long.

Really though, the goal in shmups is to get the high score - that means memorizing all the patterns and never making a mistake - and that's why I stopped playing them. That's not what I call "fun".
